lesson_title: The Stadium and the Pea: Inside the Atom
hook_text: You have never touched anything in your life. Here's the physics of why.
clip_script: Blow an atom up to the size of a soccer stadium. The nucleus — the part with nearly ALL the mass — is a single pea on the centre spot. Everything else, out to the last row of seats, is almost empty space patrolled by electrons. Your desk, your phone, your own hand: mostly nothing. So why does a desk feel solid? Because you have never actually touched it. As your hand gets close, your atoms' outer electrons meet the desk's outer electrons — negative against negative — and like charges repel. That electric push is what 'solid' feels like. You have spent your whole life pressing against force fields. And we know the pea is real: scientists fired particles at gold foil so thin it was almost nothing, and nearly all sailed straight through — empty stadium — but one in thousands bounced straight back. You only bounce off a pea if there IS a pea. That bounce discovered the nucleus, and it is where the whole of chemistry begins.
visual_style: A floodlit stadium at night with a glowing pea on the kickoff dot; camera sweeps the empty stands as faint electron sparks orbit; a hand presses toward a desk and ripples of repelling charge light up between them; alpha particles streak through gold foil, one ricocheting hard.
mood: Awe at emptiness, landing on a delicious everyday twist.
pacing: Slow zoom into the stadium, quickening sparks, a beat of silence before the you-never-touched-anything reveal, brisk gold-foil finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and meet the pea that runs the universe.
